issues.legal_issue: The central legislature had competence to enact a law whose dominant purpose was acquisition of property.
material_facts: The enactment transferred rights in the specified area to the Central Government following communal violence and the demolition of the disputed structure.
Uttar Pradesh was under President's rule when the enactment was made.
issues.conclusion: The enactment was within Parliament's legislative competence because its pith and substance was acquisition of property, not public order.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Entry 42 of List III, which covers acquisition and requisitioning of property. It relied on The State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga and Deputy Commissioner and Collector, Kamrup v. Durga Nath Sarma for identifying the pith and substance of legislation, and noted the breadth of Entry 42 after the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act.

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: A party challenges whether the central legislature had authority to enact the law.
predicates.law_substantially_acquires_property: The law's dominant purpose and substance is the acquisition of property.

issues.definition: When a legislative-competence challenge concerns a law whose dominant substance is property acquisition, the central legislature has competence.

issues.legal_issue: The acquisition scheme, including the temporary maintenance of the existing position at the disputed site, was not invalid as anti-secular or discriminatory, apart from the provision extinguishing pending proceedings.
material_facts: The acquired disputed site was held by the Central Government pending resolution of competing title claims and was to be transferred in accordance with the final adjudication.
Muslim worship had not taken place at the disputed site since at least December 1949, while Hindu worship by devotees had continued until the demolition and was thereafter restricted to a priest.
The position maintained after the acquisition did not enlarge Hindu worship beyond the reduced position existing immediately before the acquisition.
The Government stated that it would act even-handedly and implement a resolution consistent with the final determination of the dispute.
issues.conclusion: The remaining provisions of the Act were constitutionally valid on the Court's construction of them; the temporary maintenance of the existing position was not anti-secular or discriminatory.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the constitutional guarantee of equal treatment of religions and the principle that secularism is a basic feature, drawing on Articles 14, 25 and 26, the Preamble, Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala and S.R. Bommai v. Union of India. It construed Sections 3, 6 and 7 as providing limited, custodial vesting of the disputed site pending adjudication and a temporary status quo arrangement, rather than an absolute transfer of ownership.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law acquiring property connected with a dispute between religious communities.
predicates.disputed_site_held_pending_title_adjudic: The government holds the disputed site temporarily while competing claims to it await final adjudication.
predicates.status_quo_does_not_enlarge_one_communit: The maintained position preserves, rather than enlarges, the worship exercised by one community immediately before the acquisition.

issues.definition: Where a challenged acquisition holds a disputed site pending title adjudication and its temporary status quo does not enlarge one community's worship, the scheme is not invalid as anti-secular or discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: Pending suits cannot be abated without an effective alternative mechanism for deciding the dispute and preserving access to judicial redress.
material_facts: The Act abated pending suits and proceedings concerning title to the disputed property.

The Presidential Reference asked whether a Hindu temple or religious structure had existed before construction of the disputed structure, but did not cover the core title question or the defences raised in the suits.
The Government's stated plan contemplated negotiations after the Court's opinion and further action if negotiations failed; the opinion alone would not decide the title dispute.
issues.conclusion: The provision abating the pending suits was unconstitutional and invalid because no effective alternative dispute-resolution mechanism replaced them; that provision was severable from the rest of the Act.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that extinguishing the judicial remedy without substituting an effective means of resolving the dispute negates the rule of law. It relied on Article 143(1) and Smt. Indira Nehru Gandhi/Shri Raj Narain v. Shri Raj Narain/Smt. Indira Nehru Gandhi. The ruling concerned Section 4(3), which the Court severed from the remaining enactment.

predicates.challenge_to_law_abating_pending_cases: A party challenges a law that terminates pending proceedings concerning a disputed property right.
predicates.pending_title_cases_exist: Proceedings concerning the competing claims to title are pending when the law takes effect.
predicates.no_effective_alternative_decision_proces: The replacement process does not determine the core dispute and does not provide an effective alternative means of adjudication.

issues.definition: If a law terminates pending title proceedings without an effective replacement process, the termination is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of adjacent property may be valid when needed to make the outcome of adjudication effective, but property found unnecessary must be returned to its undisputed owner.
material_facts: The acquisition included adjacent property whose ownership was not disputed and which belonged in substantial part to Hindus.
The Government justified acquiring adjacent property as necessary to ensure effective access to, and enjoyment of, the disputed site by whichever party prevailed.
The Court held that the necessity of the adjacent area could be assessed after adjudication and that surplus property should then be restored to its owner.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the adjacent-area acquisition was premature; any area found superfluous after the exact need was determined had to be restored, and an owner could renew a challenge if unnecessary property continued to be retained.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated acquisition of adjacent property as permissible when incidental to the main purpose and needed to make the adjudicated result effective. It relied on M. Padmanabha Iyengar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh and Akhara Shri Braham Buta, Amritsar v. State of Punjab, while reserving a later challenge to needless retention.

predicates.challenge_to_adjacent_property_acquisiti: An owner challenges the acquisition of property adjacent to the central disputed property.
predicates.adjacent_property_may_be_needed_for_effe: The adjacent property may be needed to ensure effective access to or enjoyment of the disputed site by the party ultimately entitled to it.

issues.definition: When adjacent property may be needed to make the adjudicated result effective, its acquisition may continue until need is assessed, but property found unnecessary must be restored.

issues.legal_issue: A place of worship is not categorically immune from acquisition, provided the acquisition does not extinguish an essential and integral religious practice.
material_facts: The challenge asserted that a mosque could not be acquired because of its religious status.

The Court found that, under the law applicable in India, a mosque had no greater immunity from acquisition than other places of worship, and that prayer could be offered by Muslims in places other than a mosque.
The Court recognized that a place having particular religious significance may stand differently if its acquisition would extinguish an essential and integral part of religious practice.
issues.conclusion: A mosque is not immune from acquisition merely because it is a mosque; acquisition is permissible subject to the protection of essential and integral religious practice and the need for an unusual or extraordinary situation serving a larger national purpose.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 25 and 26 and the State's sovereign power of acquisition. It relied on Khajamian Wakf Estates v. State of Madras, Acharya Maharajshri Narendra Prasadji Anand Prasadji Maharaj v. State of Gujarat, Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, the Masjid Shahid Ganj decision as approved by the Privy Council, and the principle that a religious practice is constitutionally protected when it is essential and integral to the religion.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party argues in a constitutional challenge that a place of worship cannot be acquired by the State.
predicates.place_is_not_essential_to_religious_prac: The particular place is not an essential and integral part of practicing the religion.
predicates.acquisition_does_not_extinguish_essentia: The acquisition does not eliminate the ability to practice an essential and integral religious observance.
predicates.unusual_larger_national_purpose: The acquisition occurs in an unusual or extraordinary situation to serve a larger national purpose.

issues.definition: A place of worship is not immune from acquisition when it is not essential to religious practice, its acquisition does not extinguish essential practice, and an unusual larger national purpose is served.

issues.legal_issue: The Central Government holds the disputed site as a statutory receiver pending adjudication, must maintain the prescribed position there, and must transfer it in accordance with the final determination.
material_facts: The acquisition law empowered the Central Government to transfer the property to another authority, body or trust and required it to maintain the existing position at the disputed site.
The acquisition and the Presidential Reference were made together as part of an effort to resolve the dispute.
The pending suits were revived, and the title dispute was to be adjudicated in those suits.
The disputed site was distinct from adjacent acquired property whose vesting in the Government was absolute.
issues.conclusion: Vesting of the disputed site was limited: the Central Government held it as a statutory receiver, had to manage it while maintaining the existing position, and had to transfer it in accordance with the final adjudication. Vesting of the adjacent area was absolute. Compensation provisions applied to property absolutely vested, not to the disputed site held as receiver.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed Sections 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 in context, holding that the meaning of vesting depends on its statutory setting and that the power of transfer and duty to maintain the status quo showed limited vesting of the disputed site. It relied on Maharaj Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh for the contextual meaning of vesting.

predicates.acquisition_law_holds_disputed_property_: A law places disputed property under government control while competing claims await adjudication.
predicates.government_must_preserve_existing_positi: The government is required to manage the property without changing the position at the disputed site during the interim period.
predicates.final_title_decision_identifies_entitled: A final adjudication determines which claimant is entitled to the disputed property.

issues.definition: When government control is temporary, the existing position must be preserved, and a final decision identifies the entitled claimant, the government must hold the property as receiver and transfer it to that claimant.

issues.legal_issue: The Court may decline to answer a Presidential Reference that has become unnecessary after the judicial remedy for the underlying dispute is restored.
material_facts: The Court invalidated the provision that had abated the pending title suits, so those suits stood revived for adjudication.
The question in the Presidential Reference did not itself resolve the core title dispute.
With the suits restored, answering the Reference was unnecessary to determine the parties' rights.
issues.conclusion: The Court respectfully declined to answer the Presidential Reference and returned it as superfluous and unnecessary; it did not decide the merits of the Reference's maintainability.
issues.legal_principle: The Court acted under Article 143(1) and relied on Special Reference No. 1 of 1964 and In re the Special Courts Bill, 1978, which recognize that the Court may decline to give an advisory opinion when the circumstances make it inappropriate or unnecessary to answer.

predicates.presidential_reference_before_court: A question is referred to the Court by the President for an advisory opinion.
predicates.underlying_title_suits_are_available_for: The proceedings that can determine the parties' competing title claims remain available for adjudication.
predicates.reference_answer_would_not_resolve_core_: An answer to the referred question would not itself determine the central dispute between the parties.

issues.definition: If title suits remain available and an advisory answer would not resolve the central dispute, the Court may decline to answer the Reference as unnecessary.
